source_read: PDF of the PubMed Central author manuscript, AM pp. 1–17 (all pages; Tables 1–3 on AM pp. 13–17 checked on rendered pages). Pages are given as AM p. N (N = PDF page).

claims.overstatement: None for the Rhode Island part. Minor: 'themselves at home' is an assumption for this pilot; the paper says only that testing was unsupervised (AM p. 3) and does not say where people tested. Of the 81 analysed, 34 were told to test urine after use (AM p. 6), so for them a positive result came after the drug had been taken; how many of the 31 positives were urine tests is not reported. The statement's '(or, in one study, their urine)' covers this.
claims.note: Every Krieger figure in the statement and magnitude matches AM p. 7 (45, 42, 39, 36, 10, 10 and 7%). 45, 42, 39 and 10% fit 14, 13, 12 and 3 of 31, but 36% and 7% cannot come from 31 (11/31 = 35.5%, 2/31 = 6.5%), so some items had fewer answers, unexplained [corrected after step 2: my blind note said all seven fit 31]. 'At least two weeks later': follow-up was scheduled a minimum of two weeks after the first visit (AM p. 5; the abstract calls it a one-month visit). 'Results were not checked': AM p. 9. 'How many used as usual was not reported': 'took them anyways' was a response option (AM p. 6) but its share is never given. Not used by the claim but worth knowing: the paper's headline association (positive result linked to 'positive behaviour change', p ≤ .001 in the text, p ≤ 0.01 in the abstract) rests on a composite that is ill-defined for people without a positive result (4 of 31 such users and 6 of 19 non-users are counted as changing 'related to a fentanyl test result'), and Table 3 prints 32%/68% for 4/31 and 27/31 (should be 13%/87%); its footnote lists 'took them anyways' inside the composite of positive changes. [Added after step 2: the 62% vs 38% contrast by testing method cannot be two within-group rates, because both lie below the pooled 21/31 = 68%; it fits a split of the 21 who changed (13 and 8), as the card shows. It is not evidence that testing drugs before use led to more change than testing urine after use.]

anchors.extracted: Among the 31 who got at least one positive result (testing drugs or urine): 45% used smaller amounts, 42% went slower, 39% used with someone else around, 36% did a tester; few threw drugs out (10%), sold them (10%) or gave them away (7%). The paper says a greater share of the pre-consumption than the post-consumption group reported positive change after a positive result (62% vs 38%; see note, wording adjusted after step 2).

Behaviour change = follow-up answer to what they did after finding fentanyl, compared with baseline answers about the last time they used a drug they were confident contained fentanyl (or a hypothetical question for those unsure). Response options included did a tester, went slower, threw them out, used less, used with someone around, gave them away, sell them, took them anyways; 'positive change' = no risk-reduction answer at baseline but at least one after a positive result. The share answering 'took them anyways' is not reported.

anchors.locator: 2.1 Study Design and Recruitment, 4th paragraph (begins AM p. 4)
anchors.extracted: Follow-up visit scheduled at least two weeks after the first visit; first 40 recruits assigned to urine testing after use, the rest to testing drug residue or samples before use (34 and 47 of the 81 analysed, AM p. 6).

anchors.locator: Table 3, row 'Any positive overdose risk behavior change'
anchors.extracted: Positive change: 21/31 with a positive result vs 4/31 without (printed percentages 68 and 32; 4/31 is 13%), p < .001; strip users 25/62 (40%) vs non-users 6/19 (32%), p = .513. Footnote lists 'took them anyways' among the composite's responses.
Self-reports subject to social desirability and recall bias; reported strip results were not verified; convenience sample of young adults in Rhode Island; small sample, no multivariable analysis.

claims.note: Krieger has no group without strips and reports no responses to a negative result, consistent with the claim. Its kits came with guidance against false reassurance (negative labelled 'unknown'; told fentanyl may still be present; told to keep overdose-prevention practices regardless) plus overdose education and naloxone, so its findings describe kits given with that guidance.

anchors.extracted: Each strip carried a sticker reading 'fentanyl' for a positive and 'unknown' for a negative result; participants were told fentanyl or analogues could be present despite a negative result and instructed to follow overdose-prevention practices whatever the result; all received overdose education and a take-home intranasal naloxone kit.

Only actions after a positive result are reported; nothing on behaviour after a negative result; no comparison with people not given strips; within the cohort, behaviour change did not differ between strip users and non-users (Table 3: 40% vs 32%, p = .513).

BTNX urine strips, detection level 20 ng/ml; relayed (Johns Hopkins report) sensitivity 96% and 100% and specificity 90% and 98% at two sites against laboratory methods; detect acetylfentanyl and furanylfentanyl; show presence or absence only, not amount.

claims.note: Median 3 (IQR 1–6) and 10 (12%) using all ten match; 77/81 = 95.1%. The paper does not say whether the median is over all 81 or the 62 users (an IQR starting at 1 fits either, with 19 zeros = 23%). 58% gave strips to others (denominator not stated), so strips a person did not use were not necessarily left unused; read '3 of 10' with that in mind. The window was 'a few weeks' as stated: at least two weeks, abstract says one month, actual intervals not given.

anchors.extracted: 62 of 81 (77%) used at least one strip; median 3 strips used (IQR 1–6); 10 participants (12%; 4 pre-, 6 post-consumption) used all ten; 58% gave strips to others.
77 (95%) wanted to keep using the strips and 75 (93%) said continuing would be easy; future-use agreement 61/62 (98%) among users vs 16/19 (84%) among non-users, p = .041.

claims.overstatement: Two qualifications for the Rhode Island part. (1) The pilot gives no disposal figure after a negative result, so it contributes to 'few' but not to the comparison of unexpected with expected results. (2) A positive strip was often not unexpected here: 26 of the 31 with a positive result had already used a drug they were confident contained fentanyl (Table 2, AM p. 15). Also, the sample was not limited to people who use opioids (eligible with cocaine use or street-bought pills; 20 of the 31 positives used heroin weekly), so 'among people who use opioids' is loose for this study.
claims.note: 10% of 31 = 3 people (rounded); sold 10% and gave away 7% are other ways of getting rid of the drug that pass it on.

anchors.extracted: Of the 31 with a positive result, 10% threw their drugs out, 10% sold them, 7% gave them away; self-reported at follow-up.

anchors.locator: Table 2, row 'ever used a drug you were confident was laced with fentanyl'
anchors.extracted: Among those with a positive result 26/31 (84%) had previously used a drug they were confident contained fentanyl, vs 5/31 (16%) among users without a positive result (p < .001).
Self-report; strip results not verified.

claims.overstatement: Minor wording: '62 of the 81 who returned' — 83 returned and 81 were analysed (two excluded for missing information); better '62 of the 81 analysed (83 returned)'. Also, 34 of the 81 were told to test urine after use rather than drugs before use, so 'used at least one strip' mixes the two uses.
claims.note: Recomputed: 62/81 = 76.5% (Wilson 66.2–84.4%) and 62/93 = 66.7% (56.6–75.4%): same as the claim. Median 3 (IQR 1–6), 10 (12%) all ten, 58% gave strips to others (denominator not stated): all match. Payments $25 and $50; training by video plus naloxone kit; follow-up at least two weeks later: all match. Returners and those lost to follow-up did not differ (results not shown).

anchors.locator: 2.1 Study Design and Recruitment, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs
anchors.extracted: Interviewer survey, short video training on using and reading strips, 10 strips each with written instructions; overdose education and a take-home intranasal naloxone kit.
62 (77%) used at least one strip; median 3 (IQR 1–6); 10 (12%) used all ten; 58% gave strips to others; use more common among those who had dealt drugs (p = .038).
Analytic sample 81 (87% of 93); returners and those lost to follow-up did not differ (results not shown); 34 (42%) assigned urine testing after use, 47 (58%) drug testing before use.
Self-reported use not verified; convenience sample of young adults in Rhode Island; reasons for non-use among the 23% who did not use strips not assessed.

claims.overstatement: The Rhode Island sentence is accurate, but this study's own comparison of strip users with non-users does not support the lead sentence's 'more heroin use, more injecting, more often having seen an overdose': weekly heroin 37% vs 21% (p = .269), ever injected 47% vs 68% (p = .099, the opposite direction), ever witnessed an overdose 60% vs 63% (p = .884). The magnitude field gives the injecting figures but the statement does not; suggest saying that in the Rhode Island pilot strip users, if anything, injected less often. The heroin, injecting and witnessed-overdose differences in this study belong to getting a positive result among users, as the statement correctly says for heroin.
claims.note: Numbers check: dealt drugs 52/62 (84%) vs 11/19 (58%), p = .038 as printed, but one non-user's answer is missing (11 + 7 = 18), so 11/18 = 61% among those who answered. Positive vs no positive result: weekly heroin 20/31 (65%) vs 3/31 (10%), ever injected 25/31 (81%) vs 8/31 (26%), witnessed overdose 29/31 (94%) vs 9/31 (29%): all match Table 1. Recruitment was by advertisements and word of mouth, not at harm-reduction services, consistent with 'mostly' and 'the two larger studies'. All characteristics self-reported at baseline.

Recruited through bus and online advertisements, fliers and word of mouth (plus 4 from an earlier cohort), not at harm-reduction services; age 18–35, living in Rhode Island, past-30-day heroin, cocaine, injecting or street-bought pills.

key_findings.note: Recomputed the own-drugs row from Table 2 counts (26/31 vs 16/31): Pearson chi-square p = 0.0066, Fisher p = 0.013, as the card says, against printed .088.
Recomputed: 11/31 = 35.5% and 2/31 = 6.5%, so 36% and 7% cannot come from 31, as the card says. My blind note wrongly said all seven fit; corrected in the claim note.
Checked the logic: two within-group rates cannot both lie below their pooled 68%; 13/21 = 61.9% and 8/21 = 38.1% fit a split of the changers. I had taken the 62%/38% at face value in step 1.

reporting_issues.note: Also checked: in the two Table 2 rows named, the user column totals 60 while the positive/no-positive columns total 62.
Recomputed: own drugs p = 0.0066 (chi-square) / 0.013 (Fisher); race by positive result p = 0.30; lifetime overdose by strip use p = 0.32.

risk_of_bias.note: ROBINS-I, critical overall for any effect of strips or of a positive result on behaviour: no group without strips, unadjusted and confounded comparisons, and an outcome defined only after a positive result yet assigned to non-users. Domain judgments and wording match the instrument's vocabulary. The card is right to keep the descriptive uptake, actions and acceptability figures citable as self-reports.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial: the abstract's 'significantly associated' and the Discussion's 'preliminary evidence' rest on the confounded composite. The Conclusions' 'tool to detect IMF in illicit drugs' was never verified, and 34 of 81 tested urine after use.

missed.finding: Strip users did not use heroin more often (37% vs 21%, p = .269) or more often witness an overdose (60% vs 63%), and injected less often, non-significantly (47% vs 68%, p = .099). KF4 says only that nothing else differed significantly. The direction matters for cl_dc_uptake_who_tests, whose lead sentence says strip users inject more.
